cards.statement: Under IaaS, Microsoft maintains the physical hosts that run a customer's Azure virtual machines.
cards.explanation: In the shared responsibility model, Microsoft is responsible for the physical hosts, physical network and physical datacenter under IaaS, PaaS and SaaS alike.

cards.statement: Customers remain responsible for information and data stored in cloud services.
cards.explanation: Customers retain responsibility for their cloud data, including its classification, protection, and governance.

cards.statement: A private cloud requires the organization's datacenter to be on-site.
cards.explanation: A private cloud can run in an on-site datacenter or a dedicated datacenter off-site.
cards.misconception: Private cloud infrastructure has to be located on the organization's premises.

cards.statement: A public cloud is built and maintained by a third-party cloud provider.
cards.explanation: A third-party provider builds, controls, and maintains public cloud infrastructure that customers can purchase access to.

cards.statement: A hybrid cloud can use public cloud resources during a temporary demand spike.
cards.explanation: An interconnected public and private cloud environment can add public cloud capacity when demand temporarily exceeds private capacity.

cards.statement: Buying datacenter servers up front is classified as operational expenditure.
cards.explanation: An up-front purchase of physical servers is capital expenditure (CapEx).
cards.misconception: Up-front infrastructure purchases are operational expenditure.

cards.statement: A multicloud environment pairs one public cloud provider with an organization's own private cloud.
cards.explanation: In a multicloud scenario you use two or more public cloud providers; an environment that interconnects public and private clouds is a hybrid cloud.
cards.misconception: Multicloud means combining one public cloud with a private cloud.

cards.statement: Buying an Azure reservation moves the covered virtual machines onto separate, reserved hardware.
cards.explanation: A reservation is a billing discount for a one-year or three-year commitment; it applies automatically to matching resources, which keep running unchanged.
cards.misconception: A reservation saves money by changing how the covered resources run.

cards.statement: By default, an Azure Functions app on the Flex Consumption plan scales in to zero instances when idle.
cards.explanation: Flex Consumption is the recommended serverless plan for Azure Functions. It scales to zero, and its always-ready instances, which default to zero, are an option to cut cold starts.

source.title: Azure Functions Flex Consumption plan hosting

cards.statement: Cloud service-level agreements provide one uniform uptime guarantee across services.
cards.explanation: Service-level agreement availability commitments vary by service.
cards.misconception: Cloud services share a single uptime commitment.

source.title: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud

cards.statement: Scaling out increases the CPU and RAM allocated to an existing virtual machine.
cards.explanation: Scaling out adds resource instances. Increasing the CPU or RAM of an existing virtual machine is scaling up.
cards.misconception: Scaling out changes the size of an existing instance.

source.title: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud

cards.statement: Cloud autoscaling also scales capacity back in, removing resources once a traffic peak subsides.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Learn describes scaling in, like scaling out, as something that happens automatically or manually, so capacity added for a peak can be removed as demand falls.

source.title: Describe the benefits of high availability and scalability in the cloud

cards.statement: Cloud reliability comes from spreading resources across regions rather than hardening one central datacenter.
cards.explanation: Reliability is a system's ability to recover from failures and keep working; with resources in many regions, other regions stay up when one region has a catastrophic event.

source.title: Describe the benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud

cards.statement: Load balancing supports performance predictability by shifting traffic away from overloaded resources.
cards.explanation: Load balancing can redirect traffic toward less stressed resources, helping a workload deliver steadier performance.

source.title: Describe the benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud

cards.statement: Cloud cost predictability depends on each resource having a fixed monthly charge.
cards.explanation: Cost predictability uses resource-usage tracking and forecasts; cloud charges can vary as consumption changes.
cards.misconception: Predictable cloud costs require fixed charges for each resource.

source.title: Describe the benefits of reliability and predictability in the cloud

cards.statement: Cloud auditing offers mitigation strategies for resources out of compliance with a baseline.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Learn lists cloud auditing as a governance benefit: it flags resources that are out of compliance with your baseline and suggests ways to mitigate them.

source.title: Describe the benefits of security and governance in the cloud

cards.statement: After deployment, keeping cloud resources aligned with a changed standard falls outside the scope of templates.
cards.explanation: Templates keep deployed resources aligned with technical and regulatory standards; when a standard changes, the resources already deployed can be updated at scale.
cards.misconception: A changed governance standard has to be rolled out to each deployed resource individually.

source.title: Describe the benefits of security and governance in the cloud

cards.statement: Managing the cloud can include automatic replacement of failing resources.
cards.explanation: Cloud resource management can monitor health and automatically replace resources that fail.

source.title: Describe the benefits of manageability in the cloud

cards.statement: In IaaS, the provider patches the guest operating system on customer virtual machines.
cards.explanation: IaaS customers install, configure, and maintain the operating systems on their virtual machines.
cards.misconception: IaaS transfers guest operating system maintenance to the provider.

cards.statement: IaaS supports lift-and-shift migration of an existing server workload.
cards.explanation: Lift-and-shift can move a workload to cloud infrastructure configured similarly to its on-premises environment.

cards.statement: IaaS lets teams rapidly recreate established configurations for development and testing.
cards.explanation: Teams can start or stop IaaS development and test environments quickly while retaining control of their configurations.

cards.statement: In IaaS, the provider configures the customer's virtual network.
cards.explanation: IaaS customers configure networking for their workloads; the provider maintains the underlying physical network.
cards.misconception: The IaaS provider configures the customer's virtual networking.

cards.statement: In PaaS, the provider maintains the operating system and managed runtime.
cards.explanation: The PaaS provider manages platform components such as the operating system, middleware, and runtime.

cards.statement: PaaS can provide analytics tools for examining an organization's data.
cards.explanation: PaaS analytics services can help teams find patterns and insights in their data.

cards.statement: In SaaS, the provider maintains the delivered application's updates.
cards.explanation: A SaaS provider handles updates to the ready-made application it delivers.

cards.statement: In SaaS, the provider sets each customer's user access policies.
cards.explanation: SaaS customers manage their users and access settings for the application they use.
cards.misconception: The SaaS provider decides which customer users receive access.

cards.statement: SaaS gives customers greater control of the application stack than IaaS.
cards.explanation: IaaS gives customers more control over the workload stack. SaaS delivers a more complete application with less customer control.
cards.misconception: SaaS provides more workload-stack control than IaaS.

cards.statement: An Azure administrator deploying a regional resource picks the datacenter that hosts it.
cards.explanation: You choose a region, or a zone for a zonal resource, and Azure places the resource in a datacenter there; customers don't interact with individual datacenters.
cards.misconception: Azure deployments let the customer target an individual datacenter.

cards.statement: An Azure region contains one or more datacenters linked by a low-latency network.
cards.explanation: An Azure region groups one or more datacenters connected by a high-capacity, low-latency network.

cards.statement: Each Azure availability zone has its own independent power, cooling, and networking.
cards.explanation: Independent power, cooling, and networking make an availability zone a separate failure boundary within its region.

cards.statement: An Azure region with availability zones has at least three zones.
cards.explanation: Availability zone-enabled Azure regions have at least three zones, and some regions have more.

cards.statement: Deploying a workload in a paired Azure region provides automatic failover.
cards.explanation: A region pair does not provide automatic workload failover. The workload needs its own high availability and disaster recovery design.
cards.misconception: Region pairing automatically fails workloads over.

source.title: Azure region pairs and nonpaired regions

cards.statement: Azure Government shares its physical datacenters with global Azure.
cards.explanation: Azure Government uses physically isolated datacenters and networks located in the United States.
cards.misconception: Azure Government uses the global Azure cloud's physical facilities.

cards.statement: An Azure resource belongs to one resource group at a time.
cards.explanation: A resource can exist in only one resource group, and supported resources can be moved to another group. A few resource types are deployed at subscription, management group or tenant scope instead.

cards.statement: An Azure resource group confines its resources to one region.
cards.explanation: A resource group can contain resources deployed in different Azure regions; its own location stores the group's metadata.
cards.misconception: A resource group's location restricts the locations of its resources.

source.title: Use the Azure portal and Azure Resource Manager to manage resource groups

cards.statement: An Azure subscription serves as a billing boundary for resources.
cards.explanation: Subscriptions are billing units that can separate billing for different sets of Azure resources.

cards.statement: Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets require an operator to add each new VM when demand rises.
cards.explanation: Scale sets can use autoscale rules to add VM instances as demand rises, so an operator need not add each one.
cards.misconception: Scale sets always need manual instance additions.

source.title: Autoscale a virtual machine scale set

cards.statement: Azure availability sets distribute virtual machines across fault and update domains.
cards.explanation: An availability set spreads VMs across fault and update domains, reducing the chance that one host fault or update affects them together.

cards.statement: With Azure Virtual Desktop, an organization runs its own gateway and connection broker servers.
cards.explanation: Azure Virtual Desktop manages the gateway and broker roles for you; you manage only the session host images and VMs, unlike a Remote Desktop Services deployment.
cards.misconception: Azure Virtual Desktop needs customer-run gateway and broker servers, as Remote Desktop Services does.

cards.statement: Azure App Service can host web applications and REST APIs on a managed web platform.
cards.explanation: Azure App Service handles the hosting platform for web apps and REST APIs, letting developers focus on application code.

cards.statement: Azure Container Instances requires an Azure Kubernetes Service cluster to run a container group.
cards.explanation: Azure Container Instances runs container groups directly in Azure; an Azure Kubernetes Service cluster is optional for this service.
cards.misconception: Container Instances requires a Kubernetes cluster.

cards.statement: Azure Functions can run application code in response to an event such as a storage queue message.
cards.explanation: Azure Functions uses triggers, including queue messages, to run code when the corresponding event occurs.

cards.statement: Peering two Azure virtual networks also connects their other peered networks to each other.
cards.explanation: Virtual network peering is nontransitive: peering A to B and B to C does not by itself connect A to C.
cards.misconception: Peering through a hub gives automatic transitive connectivity.

source.title: Create, change, or delete a virtual network peering

cards.statement: Azure ExpressRoute connects on-premises networks through an encrypted tunnel over the public internet.
cards.explanation: Azure ExpressRoute uses private connectivity through a provider; Azure VPN Gateway uses encrypted VPN connections over the public internet.
cards.misconception: ExpressRoute uses the same public-internet tunnel model as VPN Gateway.

cards.statement: On-premises clients connected through VPN or ExpressRoute reach an Azure private endpoint at its private IP.
cards.explanation: A private endpoint is a network interface with a private IP from your virtual network, reachable from that network, peered networks and on-premises networks linked by VPN or ExpressRoute.

cards.statement: Azure Blob Storage exposes SMB file shares that applications can mount.
cards.explanation: Azure Files provides mountable SMB file shares; Azure Blob Storage stores object data rather than SMB shares.
cards.misconception: Blob Storage presents SMB file shares.

cards.statement: The cool tier keeps infrequently accessed Azure blobs online for immediate retrieval.
cards.explanation: The cool tier is online storage for blobs accessed less often; data remains available for immediate read access.

cards.statement: An Azure blob in the archive tier can be read immediately through its usual endpoint.
cards.explanation: Archive blobs are offline and need rehydration to an online tier before they can be read.
cards.misconception: Archive blobs remain directly readable.

cards.statement: Locally redundant storage keeps Azure Storage replicas within a single datacenter.
cards.explanation: Locally redundant storage keeps copies inside one datacenter to protect against storage hardware failures.

cards.statement: With geo-redundant storage (GRS), applications can read the secondary copy before a failover.
cards.explanation: With GRS the secondary region's data is readable or writable only after a failover; read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) allows reads from the secondary at any time.
cards.misconception: GRS gives applications read access to the secondary region at all times.

cards.statement: An Azure storage account name must be unique across all of Azure.
cards.explanation: The account name forms part of the account's endpoint URLs, such as https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net, so no two storage accounts in Azure share a name.

cards.statement: AzCopy provides a graphical interface for browsing and transferring Azure blobs.
cards.explanation: AzCopy is a command-line transfer tool; Azure Storage Explorer provides the graphical interface for browsing and transferring storage data.
cards.misconception: AzCopy is the graphical storage browser.

cards.statement: Azure File Sync can cache an Azure file share on a Windows Server for local access.
cards.explanation: Azure File Sync can keep an Azure file share synchronized with a Windows Server endpoint and cache files for local access.

cards.statement: Azure Data Box assesses the readiness of on-premises servers for migration to Azure.
cards.explanation: Azure Data Box transfers data using a physical device; Azure Migrate assesses on-premises servers for migration.
cards.misconception: Data Box assesses server migration readiness.

cards.statement: Microsoft Entra ID provides managed LDAP and Kerberos services for legacy applications.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Entra Domain Services provides managed LDAP and Kerberos for legacy applications; Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud identity service.
cards.misconception: Microsoft Entra ID directly supplies managed LDAP and Kerberos domains.

source.title: What is Microsoft Entra Domain Services?

cards.statement: The security of Microsoft Entra ID single sign-on depends on the initial authenticator used for the session.
cards.explanation: Single sign-on relies on the first authenticator when granting access to further trusted apps, so its strength affects the session.

cards.statement: Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication can challenge a user with an app notification.
cards.explanation: A mobile app notification can act as the additional sign-in factor requested by Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication.

cards.statement: Microsoft Entra ID supports FIDO2 security keys for passwordless sign-in.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID accepts FIDO2 security keys as a passwordless method, replacing a typed password at sign-in.

source.title: Passwordless authentication in Microsoft Entra ID

cards.statement: With Microsoft Entra External ID, invited partners sign in to shared resources with identities they already have.
cards.explanation: With B2B collaboration, a guest user object is added to your directory, but the partner signs in with their own work, school or social credentials.

cards.statement: An Azure RBAC role assigned to a resource group grants access across its parent subscription.
cards.explanation: An Azure RBAC assignment at resource-group scope covers that group and its resources, not the parent subscription.
cards.misconception: A resource-group role assignment extends to the parent subscription.

source.title: What is Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC)?

cards.statement: Microsoft's Zero Trust model lists defense in depth among its three guiding principles.
cards.explanation: Microsoft's Zero Trust model rests on three guiding principles: verify explicitly, use least privilege access and assume breach. Defense in depth is a separate layered approach.
cards.misconception: Defense in depth is one of the Zero Trust guiding principles.

cards.statement: In Microsoft's defense-in-depth model, the data layer sits at the center of the security layers.
cards.explanation: The model puts data at its center because the surrounding layers protect the data and access to it.

cards.statement: Microsoft Defender for Cloud limits its security recommendations to Azure-hosted resources.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Cloud assesses security posture and recommends improvements across Azure, other clouds, and hybrid resources.
cards.misconception: Defender for Cloud gives recommendations only for Azure resources.

source.title: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?

cards.statement: Azure VM prices are determined independently of the deployment region.
cards.explanation: Azure VM pricing can vary by deployment region, so choosing a region can affect the price of a similar VM.
cards.misconception: VM prices are identical across deployment regions.

source.title: Describe factors that can affect costs in Azure

cards.statement: Outbound data transfer from Azure can add a charge to a workload's bill.
cards.explanation: Azure bandwidth pricing can charge for outbound data transfer, adding cost when workload data leaves Azure.

cards.statement: Stopping an Azure VM from inside its guest OS ends its compute charges.
cards.explanation: A VM shut down from its guest OS remains Stopped (Allocated), and compute charges continue until deallocation.
cards.misconception: Guest OS shutdown ends VM compute billing.

source.title: States and billing status of Azure Virtual Machines

cards.statement: Adding a service to the Azure pricing calculator provisions it in a subscription.
cards.explanation: The Azure pricing calculator creates a cost estimate; adding a service to the estimate creates no Azure resource.
cards.misconception: The pricing calculator provisions services included in an estimate.

cards.statement: Microsoft Cost Management can group Azure costs by subscription and resource group.
cards.explanation: Cost analysis can break down costs by subscription or by resource group, helping teams attribute charges to parts of their Azure hierarchy.

source.title: Group and filter options in Cost Analysis and Budgets

cards.statement: A Microsoft Cost Management budget automatically blocks spending at its threshold.
cards.explanation: A Microsoft Cost Management budget tracks spend and can trigger threshold alerts; it does not automatically stop consumption.
cards.misconception: A Cost Management budget blocks spending when its threshold is met.

cards.statement: Microsoft Cost Management can alert on an unexpected change in daily usage.
cards.explanation: Anomaly detection compares daily usage patterns and can alert on an unexpected spike or dip.

cards.statement: Azure resource tags can group usage costs by internal cost center.
cards.explanation: Resource tags add business context to cost data, so a cost-center tag can attribute usage within a shared subscription.

source.title: Use tags to organize your Azure resources

cards.statement: A tag on an Azure resource group appears automatically in each contained resource's tags.
cards.explanation: A resource group's tags do not populate the tag properties of its contained resources; each resource has its own tags.
cards.misconception: A resource automatically inherits the tags stored on its resource group.

source.title: Use tags to organize your Azure resources

cards.statement: Microsoft Purview Data Map can catalog data sources across Azure, other clouds, and on-premises systems.
cards.explanation: Microsoft Purview Data Map supports data discovery across hybrid and multicloud environments, so teams can find sources in more than one environment.

cards.statement: A Microsoft Purview Data Map scan copies the source's data into the catalog for direct querying.
cards.explanation: A Microsoft Purview Data Map scan ingests metadata such as schemas and classifications into the catalog; it does not create a queryable copy of source data.
cards.misconception: A Data Map scan imports source datasets for querying.

source.title: Scans and ingestion in Data Map

cards.statement: An Azure Policy initiative groups several policy definitions into one assignable unit.
cards.explanation: An initiative definition is a collection of policy definitions aimed at one overall goal; assigning the initiative applies and evaluates all of its policies together.

cards.statement: Azure Policy evaluates a resource's compliance at creation and then stops checking it until the resource changes.
cards.explanation: Azure Policy also evaluates resources when a policy or initiative is assigned or changed at their scope, and in a regular standard compliance cycle, not only on create or update.
cards.misconception: Azure Policy evaluates compliance only when a resource is created.

cards.statement: Azure Policy remediation tasks can bring existing resources into compliance with a modify policy.
cards.explanation: A remediation task applies a modify policy's changes to existing noncompliant resources; evaluation alone does not update them.

source.title: Details of the policy remediation task structure

cards.statement: An Azure Policy assignment grants users permission to create resources in its scope.
cards.explanation: Azure Policy governs resource compliance. Azure RBAC grants users or identities permission to create resources within a scope.
cards.misconception: A policy assignment grants access like a role assignment.

cards.statement: A subscription Owner's role permissions override a Delete lock placed on an Azure resource.
cards.explanation: A Delete lock blocks direct deletion even for a subscription Owner. A user with the required permission can remove the lock first.
cards.misconception: Subscription Owner bypasses a Delete lock.

source.title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure

cards.statement: Resources added later to a locked resource group automatically inherit the group's lock.
cards.explanation: A lock applied at a parent scope is inherited by every resource in that scope, including resources added afterward; the most restrictive lock in the chain takes precedence.

source.title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure

cards.statement: A resource lock blocks direct data-plane writes to blobs in a protected storage account.
cards.explanation: Azure resource locks restrict control-plane operations. A lock on a storage account does not block direct data-plane writes to its blobs.
cards.misconception: A storage account lock also blocks blob data writes.

source.title: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure

cards.statement: Azure portal dashboards use one shared layout across users of a subscription.
cards.explanation: Azure portal dashboards are customizable; users have private dashboards by default and can choose to share one.
cards.misconception: A subscription has one common portal dashboard for its users.

source.title: Create a dashboard in the Azure portal

cards.statement: Azure CLI can run Azure management commands from a shell script on Linux or macOS.
cards.explanation: Azure CLI is a cross-platform command-line tool for managing Azure resources and can be used in shell scripts.

cards.statement: Azure PowerShell exposes Azure management operations as PowerShell cmdlets that return objects.
cards.explanation: Azure PowerShell provides cmdlets for managing Azure resources; their object output can be filtered or passed through PowerShell pipelines.

source.title: Choose the right Azure command-line tool

cards.statement: Azure Arc represents servers hosted on-premises or in other clouds as resources in Azure Resource Manager.
cards.explanation: Azure Arc extends Azure management to servers outside Azure, including on-premises and other cloud environments, so they can be organized and governed like Azure resources.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager templates record a sequence of manual steps to create each resource.
cards.explanation: Azure Resource Manager templates declare the desired Azure resources and properties; Resource Manager orchestrates their deployment.
cards.misconception: ARM templates describe a step-by-step manual procedure.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager processes deployment requests differently in the portal and Azure CLI.
cards.explanation: Azure Resource Manager is the common management layer for requests sent through the Azure portal and Azure CLI.
cards.misconception: Portal and CLI deployments use separate management engines.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager deployment templates use JSON for their resource definitions and parameters.
cards.explanation: The template format is JSON; Azure Resource Manager reads its resource definitions and parameters during deployment.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager executes Bicep source files directly as deployment templates.
cards.explanation: When you deploy a Bicep file, the Bicep CLI first converts it into an Azure Resource Manager template, and Resource Manager then deploys that template.
cards.misconception: Resource Manager runs Bicep source directly rather than converting it.

cards.statement: Azure Resource Manager template deployments can target a resource group or a subscription.
cards.explanation: An ARM template deployment can target multiple Azure scopes, including a resource group and a subscription.

source.title: How to use ARM deployment templates with Azure CLI

cards.statement: Azure Advisor groups recommendations under cost, security, performance, reliability, and operational excellence.
cards.explanation: Azure Advisor analyzes deployed Azure resources and organizes its improvement recommendations into these categories.

cards.statement: Azure Advisor can estimate cost savings for virtual machines you plan to deploy in the future.
cards.explanation: Azure Advisor cost recommendations analyze existing resources, such as underused virtual machines, and estimate potential savings.
cards.misconception: Advisor bases VM cost recommendations on undeployed plans.

source.title: Optimize virtual machine (VM) or virtual machine scale set (VMSS) spend by resizing or shutting down underutilized instances

cards.statement: Azure Service Health can alert subscribers to planned maintenance affecting their services.
cards.explanation: Azure Service Health provides a personalized view of Azure events and can send alerts about planned maintenance.

cards.statement: Azure status shows incidents filtered to the signed-in user's Azure subscriptions.
cards.explanation: Azure status shows a public, global view of Azure service issues; Azure Service Health provides a subscription-specific view.
cards.misconception: Azure status is a personalized subscription dashboard.

cards.statement: Azure Monitor platform metrics for a virtual machine require an agent inside the guest OS.
cards.explanation: Azure Monitor collects platform metrics automatically from Azure resources. A guest OS agent is needed for guest metrics, not platform metrics.
cards.misconception: VM platform metrics require an agent in the guest OS.

source.title: Azure Monitor supported metrics and data collection

cards.statement: A diagnostic setting on an Azure resource sends its resource logs to destinations such as a Log Analytics workspace.
cards.explanation: Resource logs aren't collected by default. A diagnostic setting picks the log categories to collect and sends them to destinations such as a Log Analytics workspace, a storage account or an event hub.

source.title: Collect resource logs from an Azure resource

cards.statement: Log Analytics can run Kusto Query Language queries against Azure Monitor log data.
cards.explanation: Log Analytics uses Kusto Query Language to explore and analyze data in a Log Analytics workspace.

cards.statement: Azure Monitor alert rules are limited to metric signals, such as a VM's CPU percentage crossing a threshold.
cards.explanation: Alert rules can use metrics, log search queries or activity log events as signals; when a rule's condition is met, the alert fires and starts its action group.
cards.misconception: Azure Monitor alerts work only on metrics.

cards.statement: Azure Monitor Application Insights requires a web app to run on Azure App Service.
cards.explanation: Azure Monitor Application Insights can monitor applications hosted on Azure, on-premises, or other clouds; Azure App Service hosting is optional.
cards.misconception: Application Insights works only for apps hosted on Azure App Service.
